navVsPrice.title: NAV per Share vs Share Price
navVsPrice.content:
Net Asset Value (NAV) per share is the fair value of the trust's underlying emerging-markets equity portfolio divided by shares outstanding. The share price is what the market actually pays for that NAV on the London Stock Exchange (converted to GBP pence here).

For TEMIT: a 5-for-1 share sub-division on 26 July 2021 means FY2017-FY2020 are shown here split-adjusted (divided by 5) so the series is continuous and comparable across the split; the trust's own raw pre-split figures are 5x these (FY2017 NAV 763p raw = 152.6p split-adjusted, matching the DCF's own cross-check). The gap between the two lines IS the discount to NAV — see the Discount to NAV chart.

What to watch:

  • NAV growth is driven by the EM equity portfolio, not by any operations of the company itself
  • The 1-Sep-2026 daily NAV (351.03p, unaudited) is well above the FY2026 year-end audited NAV (267.3p) after a sharp EM/semiconductor rally — always check which NAV a price comparison uses
  • Persistent gap = market discount; a narrowing gap is a source of return independent of NAV performance

discount.title: Discount to NAV
discount.content:
The percentage by which the share price sits below (negative) or above (positive) NAV per share. This is the key valuation metric for a closed-end trust — unlike an operating company, the 'fair value' of the assets (NAV) is disclosed directly, so price/NAV plays the role P/E plays elsewhere.

For TEMIT: the discount has ranged -7.7% (FY2021, narrowest) to -15.4% (FY2024, widest) over the past decade, averaging -11.3%. It closed FY2026 at -8.2% and was ~-9.1% as of 1-Sep-2026 — inside the historical range but not at either extreme. The Board itself calls the trust's historic discount 'unsatisfactory' and has committed a £300m buyback, a 5.00p dividend floor and a conditional tender offer to address it, none of which guarantee closure.

What to watch:

  • Buybacks executed inside the discount are NAV-accretive to remaining holders (FY2026: 0.8% accretion from £166.2m of buybacks at an average 10.2% discount)
  • A widening discount can erase NAV gains from the holder's realised return even when the manager is outperforming
  • The conditional tender offer (up to 25% of shares at NAV-2%) only triggers if 5-yr NAV total return to 31-Mar-2029 underperforms the MSCI EM benchmark — currently on track NOT to trigger

navReturn.title: NAV Total Return vs MSCI EM Benchmark
navReturn.content:
NAV total return (dividends reinvested) measures the manager's actual investment performance, independent of the discount. Comparing it to the MSCI Emerging Markets Index (net dividends, GBP) isolates manager skill (alpha) from the EM asset class's own return.

For TEMIT: FY2026 delivered +41.3% NAV total return vs +26.8% for the benchmark, a +14.5pp outperformance driven by the trust's AI/semiconductor overweight (TSMC, SK Hynix, Samsung, MediaTek together ~33% of NAV). The 5-year record is a more sober +6.7%/yr vs the benchmark's +4.6%/yr (+2.05pp/yr alpha); FY2026 is a single exceptional year, not the through-cycle run rate the DCF extrapolates.

What to watch:

  • Concentration risk: the semiconductor overweight that drove FY2026's alpha is also the biggest single risk to it reversing
  • FY2022's -17.3% vs benchmark -6.8% shows the drawdown side of the same concentrated, high-conviction style
  • Persistent alpha justifies the ~0.86-0.97% ongoing charges; persistent underperformance would not

Portfolio composition (31 March 2026, from the FY2026 Annual Report):

Top 10 holdings (~47.7% of NAV): TSMC 16.6% (Taiwan, IT), SK Hynix 7.2% (Korea, IT), Samsung Electronics 6.5% (Korea, IT), Prosus 3.2% (China/HK Tencent proxy), ICICI Bank 2.6% (India), Grupo Financiero Banorte 2.5% (Mexico), MediaTek 2.4% (Taiwan), Itaú Unibanco 2.3% (Brazil), Petrobras 2.2% (Brazil), Tencent 2.2% (China/HK).

Country weight vs MSCI EM benchmark: China/HK 23.4% (bench 25.5%, underweight), Taiwan 23.0% (bench 22.5%, overweight), South Korea 22.0% (bench 15.5%, overweight +6.5pp), Brazil 9.5% (bench 5.1%, overweight +4.4pp), India 8.5% (bench 12.6%, underweight -4.1pp), South Africa 3.1%, Mexico 2.5%, US (EM-revenue names) 2.0%, Thailand 1.3%, Hungary 1.1%, Chile 1.1%.

High-conviction, bottom-up, low-turnover (typically <20%/yr) stock picker; 50-100 stocks, 12% single-issuer limit. The Korea and Brazil overweights and the semiconductor concentration (TSMC + SK Hynix + Samsung + MediaTek ~33% of NAV) are the biggest single drivers of the alpha shown in the chart above, and the biggest single risk if the theme reverses.

ongoingCharges.title: Ongoing Charges Ratio
ongoingCharges.content:
The trust's total annual running costs (management fee plus other operating costs) as a percentage of net assets — the closed-end fund equivalent of an expense ratio. Every basis point compounds directly against NAV per share.

For TEMIT: OCR has fallen steadily from 1.22% (FY2016) to 0.86% (FY2026) as net assets have grown into a tiered fee structure, and steps down further to roughly 0.70% from 1 July 2026 under a new AIFM fee of 1.0% on the first £1bn of net assets and 0.5% above (blended 0.66% at £3.2bn plus ~0.05% other costs). This fee cut is not yet reflected in the FY2026 print.

What to watch:

  • OCR falling as NAV grows is a structural tailwind to net NAV total return, built into the base-case DCF assumption
  • A market drawdown that shrinks NAV pushes OCR back up (more of the portfolio sits in the 1.0% fee band)

netAssets.title: Net Assets
netAssets.content:
Total shareholders' equity — the pool of capital represented by NAV per share times shares outstanding. For a trust this is simply the mark-to-market value of the listed EM equity portfolio, net of the small RCF drawing.

For TEMIT: net assets have been volatile with the EM cycle (peaking near £2.6bn in FY2021 and FY2026, troughing at £1.78bn in FY2020) but the underlying driver is entirely portfolio mark-to-market, not retained operating earnings — there is no operating business here.

What to watch:

  • Net assets alone conflates NAV/share growth with the share count shrinking from buybacks — always read alongside Shares Outstanding
  • Log scale used because absolute levels vary widely across the EM cycle

sharesOutstanding.title: Shares Outstanding
sharesOutstanding.content:
The number of ordinary shares in issue (excluding treasury shares). For most operating companies a falling share count signals buybacks; for TEMIT it is a deliberate, disclosed capital-return tool that mechanically boosts NAV per share for remaining holders when done at a discount.

For TEMIT: the FY2020-to-FY2021 jump from 242m to 1,181m shares is the 5-for-1 sub-division (26 July 2021), not new share issuance — the underlying economic interest was unchanged. From that post-split base the count has fallen from 1,181m (FY2021) to 945m (1-Sep-2026, ex-treasury), an ~20% reduction, entirely via the buyback programme now targeting up to £300m more over 12-24 months.

What to watch:

  • Buybacks are modelled in the DCF as a NAV-per-share accretion line, not a share-count path — the count is held flat in projections because the accretion is already captured in the return assumption
  • A widening discount makes each buyback pound more accretive; a narrowing discount makes buybacks less powerful as a lever

capitalReturn.title: Share Buybacks vs Dividends Paid
capitalReturn.content:
The two forms of cash TEMIT returns to shareholders: on-market share repurchases (which retire shares and lift NAV per share for remaining holders) and the ordinary dividend (paid from portfolio income).

For TEMIT: buybacks have grown sharply, from £3.6m (FY2022, a quiet year) to £166.2m (FY2026), with a further £300m committed over the next 12-24 months — now the larger of the two capital-return channels by far. Dividends have grown from £40.0m (FY2018) to £51.7m (FY2026) under a policy of at least 5.00p/share, fully covered by revenue earnings (5.39p/share FY2026).

What to watch:

  • Buybacks are discretionary and discount-dependent (bigger when the discount is wide); dividends are policy-anchored at a floor
  • Both reduce NAV in absolute terms but buybacks are per-share accretive when executed inside the discount, unlike dividends

gearing.title: Gearing (Net Debt / Net Assets)
gearing.content:
Net borrowings (the revolving credit facility drawn less cash) as a percentage of net assets. Closed-end trusts can gear up to amplify returns; TEMIT runs this very lightly.

For TEMIT: gearing has stayed low and often near zero (0.0% FY2024, peaking at 2.4% FY2019), currently 1.2% (£110.7m RCF drawn against £3.2bn net assets at 1-Sep-2026). Because NAV per share is already stated net of this drawing, the valuation model does NOT subtract net debt a second time — doing so would double-count it.

What to watch:

  • Low, stable gearing means no solvency or refinancing risk to the valuation — the bear case is a market/discount drawdown, not balance-sheet stress

dcf.base_sublabel: Year-5 exit value = NAV x (1 - exit discount), not an owner-FCF terminal value
dcf.model_approach_note: TEMIT is a closed-end investment trust with no operating cash flow — the DCF JSON carries a NAV + exit-discount model, not an owner-FCF DCF, so it has no FCF fields and the slider engine correctly resolves no family (sliders show stored scenario values but do not recompute). The valuation is anchored on the 1 September 2026 daily NAV of 351.03p (unaudited NZX announcement), not the stale 31 March 2026 audited NAV of 267.3p: NAV rose ~31% between March and September on an EM/semiconductor rally, so using the year-end figure against today's price would show a spurious ~19% premium instead of the real ~9.1% discount. Refresh the NAV input from the NZX daily NAV feed before relying on the upside figure for more than a few weeks.
